name: Umar Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I frame houses. New builds on estates, mostly three-bed semis for a regional housebuilder. There's four of us in the crew, Gary's the foreman, and we put up the timber frame, the joists and the roof trusses before the bricklayers come in behind us. I like a roof going on, that's the best day. Worst is wind, because you can't lift sheets in a gale and the programme doesn't care.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your routine outside the work itself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Same every day, which suits me. Van at six, bacon roll from the café by the roundabout, on site by seven. My girlfriend Rosa works at a dentist's, and we're saving for a deposit, so we've got about five months of bills put by that's meant to be the start of it. I've got an old phone that does calls and messages, and Rosa does anything online for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so. Gary's been going on about robots for a year and I'd remind him. Online, nothing, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means I carry on. Build houses, save the deposit, buy a house in a couple of years. That's the plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep framing with Gary's crew. Keep putting about two hundred a month in the deposit pot. Same van, same café, nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Good, actually. I don't like change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Gary say about robots, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He watches videos of machines that build walls and sends them to the group chat. Rosa reads them out to me sometimes. I always say, show me one on a muddy site in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want AI to help with, if it's only small stuff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe the office could stop sending us the wrong trusses. That's a person problem though, not a computer one.

S0.say: I'd say told you so, and remind Gary he's been going on about robots for a year. I'm not online, so nothing there.
S0.think: It means I carry on building houses, saving the deposit and buying a house in a couple of years. That's the plan anyway.
S0.do: Keeps framing with the same crew and keeps putting about two hundred a month into the deposit pot. Changes nothing about his routine.
S0.feel: Fine, even good, because he doesn't like change.
S0.quote: I always say, show me one on a muddy site in January.
S0.fieldNote: Umar speaks in short, plain sentences and likes his routine. He's never used AI and gets online news through his girlfriend. He'd be pleased to be proved right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll take years to reach building sites, so don't worry yet. That's what I'd tell the crew. Maybe the office lot should worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, frames already come pre-made from the factory on some estates, so it's not nothing. If more of it's done in a factory, there's less framing on site. I'd be keeping an eye on whether Gary gets fewer jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big at first. I'd keep working and put a bit more in savings, maybe two fifty instead of two hundred. If someone said I had to learn a new gadget, I'd do it, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. It's like hearing a noise in the van engine. Probably fine, but you notice it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said frames already come from factories. Have you seen that affect your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year one estate went all factory panels and we only did the roofs. Gary found us another job, so it was fine. But it was the first time I thought, oh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider working in one of those factories?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if that's where the work was. But it's indoors and the same thing all day. I'd rather be outside, even in the wind.

S1.say: I'd tell the crew it'll take years to reach building sites, so don't worry yet. Maybe the office people should worry.
S1.think: Frames already come pre-made on some estates, so there'd be less framing on site. I'd watch whether Gary gets fewer jobs.
S1.do: Keeps working and raises his savings from two hundred to two hundred and fifty a month. Would learn a new gadget only if he had to.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like an odd noise from the van engine.
S1.quote: Gary found us another job, so it was fine. But it was the first time I thought, oh.
S1.fieldNote: Publicly he plays it down, but he's already seen factory panels cut his work on one estate. His response is small and quiet: a little more saving. He'd rather stay outside than move to a factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and nobody voted for it. To the crew I'd say keep your heads down and keep working while there's work. I wouldn't say much else, I'm not one for speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the house goes. Not this house, the one we're saving for. If my job's gone in two years, no bank's giving me a mortgage, and five months of bills is five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rosa we stop the deposit plan and keep the money as a cushion instead. I'd cut the football season ticket and the weekends away. I'd keep working every hour Gary gives me and put every extra bit away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I wouldn't sleep. I'd be up checking the bank app on Rosa's phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Rosa be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. She's been looking at houses on her phone every night for a year. I'd say we're not giving up, we're just waiting, but I don't know if I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn a gadget only if you had to. Would you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it kept me in work, yeah. But I don't think it would, not in two years. I'm not a computer person, and they'd want the young lads who are.

S2.say: I'd say it's mad and nobody voted for it. I'd tell the crew to keep their heads down and keep working while there's work.
S2.think: The house we're saving for goes, because no bank lends to someone whose job is gone in two years. Five months of bills is only five months.
S2.do: Stops the deposit plan with his girlfriend and keeps the money as a cushion. Cuts the football season ticket and weekends away, works every hour offered and saves every extra bit.
S2.feel: Bad. He wouldn't sleep and would keep checking the bank balance.
S2.quote: She's been looking at houses on her phone every night for a year.
S2.fieldNote: For Umar the threat is first about the house, not the job. He shrinks his life rather than reaching for something new, and doubts he'd be picked for any new work. He says little in public and a lot at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still quick, but there's a bit of time. I'd tell the crew not to do anything daft like buy a new van on finance. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think, do we still buy the house or not? Five years is a mortgage that you can't pay after five years. I'd probably put it off and see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, but call it savings, not a deposit. Maybe go up to three hundred a month. I'd wait a year or two to see if the robots are actually any good before I change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd be getting on with it. Like a job running late, you just keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Rosa might want to go ahead with the house. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd argue about it, probably. She's braver with money than me. I'd probably give in if we found somewhere cheap and she kept her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any job you'd think about learning in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a crane ticket, or a forklift. Something still on site. But a robot can drive a forklift too, can't it. So I don't know.

S3.say: I'd say five years is still quick but there's a bit of time. I'd tell the crew not to do anything daft like buy a new van on finance.
S3.think: I'd be torn about buying the house, because a mortgage you can't pay after five years is no good. I'd probably put it off and see.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving, raising it to about three hundred a month and calling it savings rather than a deposit. Waits a year or two to see whether the robots are any good before changing anything.
S3.feel: Worried but getting on with it, like a job running late.
S3.quote: Five years is a mortgage that you can't pay after five years.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't push him to retrain; it just gives him more time to wait and save. He's honest that his girlfriend is braver with money. He thinks about other site tickets but quickly talks himself out of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's ages. I'd tell the crew it's someone else's problem for now. Probably make a joke about being retired by then, which I won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd buy the house. Ten years of a wage is a lot of mortgage paid. I'd worry about it later, maybe year five or six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, buy the house with Rosa in the next year or two, and keep a few months in the bank. I'd wait and see how it goes before doing anything else. Maybe the crane ticket if Gary needs one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like knowing the van's due its yearly test next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry later. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary losing a contract. That's my alarm bell. If he loses one to a robot outfit, I'd know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if that happened in year six, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell the house maybe, or rent a room out. I don't know. That's why I'd keep the savings, so there's time to think.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is ages and tell the crew it's someone else's problem for now. Probably joke about being retired by then.
S4.think: I'd go ahead and buy the house, because ten years of wages pays a lot of mortgage. I'd worry about it later, maybe year five or six.
S4.do: Keeps working, buys a house with his girlfriend in the next year or two and keeps a few months' savings. Waits to see how things go, perhaps taking a crane ticket if the foreman needs one.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy, like knowing the van's yearly test is due next year.
S4.quote: Gary losing a contract. That's my alarm bell.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years flips his decision on the house back to yes. His early warning is entirely practical: his foreman losing work to a robot firm. He still has no plan beyond savings and waiting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years. No time to do anything, and the house is gone. What would help is a mortgage holiday or something, so people like me don't lose the house, and some sort of wage while you look for work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Probably why I don't use the computer stuff. It's not that I'm thick, I just don't trust it. If it all comes in, I'd want someone to show me face to face, not an app.

headlineQuote: It's not that I'm thick, I just don't trust it.
portrait: Umar Silva is a 27-year-old framer on new-build housing estates, part of a four-man crew, who never uses AI and lets his girlfriend Rosa handle anything online. They have about five months of bills saved toward a house deposit. He's calm if AI fizzles and only quietly uneasy with steady change, though factory panels have already taken some of his work. AGI in two years would kill the house plan and keep him awake, while five years makes him wait and ten years lets him buy the house and worry later. He meets each picture by saving and waiting rather than learning something new.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to do anything and the house plan would be gone.
whatWouldHelp: A mortgage holiday so people don't lose their homes, some wage while looking for work, and someone to show him new things face to face.
